The Eastern tube-nosed bat Nyctimene robinsoni, a pteropodid frugivore endemic to the rainforests of northeastern Australia, exhibits a suite of life-history traits that reflect its relatively slow pace of life. Among these, the basal metabolic rate of this species has been measured at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], revealing a maximum oxygen consumption of 54.70 milliliters per hour [JOi = 54.70 milliliters per hour]. This value, characteristic of a frugivorous diet with its associated low protein content, aligns with the relatively modest energetic demands of a bat weighing around 56 grams [Wwi = around 56 grams] at adulthood as a female. Field studies tracking marked individuals indicate that a female typically brings a single pup to term once per year, a reproductive rate that translates to one litter annually. The neonates are notably altricial, entering the world at a mere 4.1 grams [Wwb = 4.1 grams], a birth mass that necessitates an extended period of intense maternal investment through lactation before the young can achieve independence.

Gestation in Nyctimene robinsoni proceeds over a substantial period, with embryonic development requiring approximately 99 days [tg = approximately 99 days] when the mother maintains a typical core body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This protracted gestation, which is among the longer durations recorded for pteropodid bats of comparable body size, is likely linked to the energetic constraints imposed by a fruit-based diet and the need to allocate resources towards the developing fetus while simultaneously meeting the female's own metabolic overhead. Following parturition, the neonatal bat enters a period of complete dependency, relying entirely on the mother's milk for its nutritional needs. The transition to nutritional independence, marked by the cessation of suckling and the onset of solid food consumption, occurs after the young has spent about 91 days since birth [tx = about 91 days since birth] under this same thermal at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]regime.

Sexual maturation in this species is a delayed process, with individuals not attaining reproductive competence until they are roughly 273 days since birth [tp = roughly 273 days since birth], a duration measured at the species' active body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This postponement of puberty, which represents a significant fraction of the animal's total lifespan, suggests that a considerable period is required for the accumulation of sufficient body condition and the development of the necessary foraging skills to support the high energetic costs associated with reproduction. The delay is especially pronounced in females, who must achieve a critical threshold of body mass and fat reserves before ovulation can occur. The subsequent transition to a reproductive adult involves first ovulation and the establishment of a regular estrous cycle, marking the beginning of the bat's potential contribution to the next generation. This life-history schedule contrasts with that of smaller, more fecund bats that may mature in a matter of months.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Eastern tube-nosed bat, extrapolated from mark-recapture studies on congeneric species, provides an upper boundary on the species' demographic potential. Individuals are estimated to live for up to approximately 10.1 years [am = up to approximately 10.1 years] under the thermal conditions typical of their natural environment, which is 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This longevity, which is substantial for a mammal of its body size, is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes high adult survival and repeated, low-effort reproductive events over a single, high-investment breeding attempt. The annual survival rate of adults is high, and the species' slow pace of life is further evidenced by its protracted developmental stages. Comparative data from the related Dobsonia moluccensis, which shares a similar dietary niche, have been used to inform this estimate, underscoring the utility of phylogenetic comparisons when direct demographic data are sparse for a particular species.

The interplay between body size, metabolic rate, and reproductive output shapes the overall life-history strategy of Nyctimene robinsoni. The mature female's wet weight of approximately 56 grams [Wwi = approximately 56 grams] represents the upper end of the typical range of 42 to 56 grams recorded in field surveys across the species' distribution. This adult mass, in concert with the high metabolic cost of flight and the low caloric density of fruit, constrains the maximum annual reproductive rate. The species' strategy of producing a single offspring per year, which is equivalent to one pup per litter [N_R_i = one pup per litter] and one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year], represents a balance between the demands of gestation and lactation and the need for the mother to maintain her own body condition through the lean season. This low fecundity, combined with a delayed age at first reproduction and an extended lifespan, positions the Eastern tube-nosed bat as a classic K-selected organism, adapted to the stable but resource-limited environment of the Australasian tropical rainforest.
